perspective:
Available to Mason Hurley:

- I am Mason Hurley, an accountant at a small community center. I work with Martha Moua, a personal care aide; we are colleagues, not personally close, and interact mainly about work.
- I reviewed the community center’s financial reports and noticed discrepancies. I suspected Martha might be mismanaging funds, which made me suspicious and anxious.
- I asked Martha to discuss the recent financial report. I told her the numbers didn’t add up, especially healthcare expenses being unusually high compared with usual spending.
- Martha said there was likely a reasonable explanation and asked what discrepancies I meant. I showed her the section. She said it might be a misentry and that she would review and correct any errors.
- After reviewing it with Martha, I concluded the discrepancies were a simple clerical error, not mismanagement. I felt relieved but embarrassed.
- I told Martha I appreciated her quick clarification and that it seemed to be a clerical error. She said errors happen and she was glad we cleared it up.
- I apologized for my initial suspicion and said I should have asked her first. Martha said it was okay, understood I was being thorough, and suggested double-checking entries next time.
- I came to believe Martha was competent, but that recurring clerical errors showed the current financial management system was inadequate. I felt frustrated with the system and empathetic toward Martha.
- I told Martha the issue wasn’t her management but the current system. I suggested a new, more robust financial system, said I would draft a proposal, and asked for her input. She agreed to help address the gaps.
- I drafted the proposal. I was hopeful about its benefits but uncertain whether management would approve or implement it.
- I told Martha I had finished the draft, believed it would benefit operations, and wasn’t sure how management would receive it. She called it solid and said to present it confidently.
- I said I would prepare a detailed presentation and asked Martha to help gather data to strengthen our case. She agreed.
- I presented the proposal to management. I felt satisfied with my efforts but physically and mentally exhausted, believing I had done everything I could.
- I told Martha the presentation went well and that it was now up to management. She praised me and suggested I take time off. I thanked her, said I would take a few days off to recharge and reflect, and hoped for good news. She told me to enjoy the break and let her know if I needed anything.
